questions.question: Which extra property turns a commutative ring with identity into a field?
options: Every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse
Every element has a distinct additive generator
The addition law becomes intentionally noncommutative
The modulus notation is replaced by polynomial syntax
questions.explanation: A field is a commutative ring with 0 != 1 where every nonzero element is invertible. Additive structure alone is not enough.

questions.question: What construction usually creates a finite extension field from a base field F?
options: F[x]/(f(x)) using an irreducible polynomial f
F[x]/(f(x)) using any polynomial with degree one
F[x] with no quotient and ordinary multiplication
F[x]/(0) with coefficients copied from integers
questions.explanation: A finite algebraic extension can be built as F[x]/(f(x)) when f is irreducible. Reducible choices produce quotient rings with zero divisors.

questions.question: Why is Z/pZ a field when p is prime?
options: Each nonzero residue is coprime to p and invertible
Each residue becomes a generator of the additive group
The product of two residues is never reduced modulo p
The multiplication table stops needing an identity
questions.explanation: When p is prime, every nonzero residue has gcd(a, p) = 1, so Extended Euclid gives an inverse modulo p.

questions.question: What goes wrong when a quotient F[x]/(f) uses reducible f?
options: Nonzero cosets can multiply to the zero coset
Addition loses closure for all coefficient pairs
The quotient contains no polynomial representatives
The base field characteristic changes after reduction
questions.explanation: If f factors, the quotient has nonzero zero divisors. It is still a quotient ring, but not a field.

questions.question: In F_p[u]/(u^2 - beta), what does beta being a quadratic non-residue imply for odd prime p?
options: The polynomial u^2 - beta has no root in F_p
The symbol u is equal to a fixed residue in F_p
The quotient has exactly p elements in total
The norm of every element is forced to equal one
questions.explanation: For a quadratic polynomial over a field, having no root means irreducible. That makes the quadratic quotient a field.

questions.question: How are elements represented in the lesson's quadratic extension code?
options: As pairs (a, b) meaning a + b times u
As decimal strings joined by a separator
As matrices whose entries store powers of p
As integers reduced only after serialization
questions.explanation: The code represents a + bu as the pair (a, b). Addition is component-wise and multiplication applies the rule u^2 = beta.

questions.question: What role does the norm play in quadratic extension inversion?
options: It gives the base-field denominator after conjugation
It chooses the display order for extension elements
It replaces addition with a new binary operation
It turns every reducible quotient into a field
questions.explanation: For x = a + bu, x times its conjugate is a^2 - beta b^2 in the base field. Inversion divides the conjugate by that norm.

questions.question: Why do pairing libraries often build field towers such as F_p^2, F_p^6, and F_p^12?
options: Tower fields make extension arithmetic structured and fast
Tower fields remove the need for base-field parameters
Tower fields make every polynomial modulus acceptable
Tower fields change finite fields into real vector spaces
questions.explanation: Tower representations preserve the extension structure and let implementations optimize arithmetic layer by layer.
